title: Fractal basin geometry and the limits to predictability and reproducibility in deep learning - Nature Machine Intelligence

AbstractFundamental limits to predictability are central to our understanding of many physical and computational systems. In deep learning, training outcomes are often difficult to predict and reproduce even when extrinsic sources of randomness are controlled, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Here we propose riddled basin geometry as a unifying dynamical systems mechanism: every initialization leading to one solution lies arbitrarily close to initializations leading to different solutions, forming a fat fractal with structure at arbitrarily fine scales. Using a minimal neural network model, we analytically establish the classical route to riddling and derive a near-zero uncertainty exponent: even sharp increases in initialization precision yield only marginal gains in outcome predictability. In deep networks, intertwined training destinations and near-zero parameter-space exponents provide robust signatures consistent with riddling across the tested architectures, optimizers and training protocols, offering a common dynamical account of otherwise disparate empirical observations. We further introduce functional uncertainty exponents, extending these diagnostics of scale-insensitive irreproducibility from parameter space to the learned functions themselves. Together, our results support riddled basin geometry as a candidate organizing principle for irreproducibility in deep learning, with practical implications for optimization and the reliable deployment of artificial intelligence.

Statistical Mechanics of Neural Network Learning and Models

MainFundamental limits to predictability are central to physics and computation, from the probabilistic outcomes of quantum measurement1, to the finite forecast horizons of chaotic systems2, to the undecidability of the halting problem in universal computation3. An equally important question confronts modern artificial intelligence (AI): What intrinsic limits constrain the predictability and hence reproducibility of training outcomes, even when all extrinsic randomness is controlled? Outcomes that cannot be predicted with certainty are seldom reproduced reliably4; unpredictability and irreproducibility are therefore tightly linked. Addressing these intrinsic limits is essential for both understanding AI systems and their practical deployment.A large body of work attributes the unpredictability of training outcomes to extrinsic stochasticity5,6,7,8,9,10,11, including random initialization, mini-batch ordering, data augmentation and numerical errors introduced by the computing platform (for example, GPU). These studies primarily measure the impact of such noise sources, showing that irreproducibility is challenging to alleviate across diverse architectures and tasks. Surprisingly, however, empirical evidence indicates that even when extrinsic non-determinism is eliminated, changing a parameter by as little as one bit can produce variability comparable to that arising from multiple noise sources combined12. The mechanism by which such vanishing perturbations yield qualitatively different training outcomes remains unclear, and the deeper question of what intrinsic limits exist on predicting training outcomes remains unaddressed.Here, we propose riddled basin geometry as a unifying dynamical systems mechanism for this unpredictability: the basins of attraction that govern training outcomes in parameter space are intertwined, such that any initialization leading to one solution lies arbitrarily close to initializations leading to a different solution13,14 (Fig. 1), reflecting a ‘fat’ fractal organization. This differs from previously reported trainability boundaries involving ‘skinny’ fractals of zero Lebesgue measure15, where predictability is recoverable by sufficiently decreasing the uncertainty, ε, of the initial conditions. By contrast, fat fractality makes a riddled basin inseparable from its boundary, so that no increase in precision restores reliable prediction of the training outcome. Riddling thus entails a form of unpredictability that goes beyond the chaotic behaviour emphasized in recent studies16,17,18: chaos limits trajectory-level predictability, with small errors in the initial conditions growing over time, whereas riddling yields qualitative, outcome-level unpredictability that persists under arbitrarily small uncertainty4,19.Fig. 1: Schematic of riddled basins and outcome unpredictability.Full size imagea, The basin of attractor A (blue) is riddled with that of attractor B (orange). Arrows indicate successive magnifications centred on the white cross; the final panel zooms in on the boxed region, revealing interleaved fractal structure at arbitrarily fine scales. b, The fractal structure is quantified by f(ε), the probability that a random perturbation of magnitude ε changes the basin. Dots and error bars represent the mean and 95% confidence intervals from n = 104 ε-close pairs (that is, pairs of initializations separated by at most ε in each dimension). A near-zero uncertainty exponent ϕ, defined by f(ε) ∝ εϕ, indicates that increasing the precision of the initialization yields only marginal gains in predictability; the qualitative fate of a given initialization (A or B?) remains effectively unpredictable, thus undermining reproducibility.Source dataWe first illustrate how riddling can emerge in learning dynamics, using a minimal model that analytically links properties widespread in deep learning, including symmetries20 and convergence towards symmetry-induced invariant subspaces21. To quantify fine-scale fractal structure, we adapt uncertainty exponents from dynamical systems theory22,23. We find near-zero exponents consistent with riddled basin geometry, indicating that reproducibility does not materially improve with increasing initialization precision. We then generalize to the parameter space of deep networks, showing that the same riddling-like signatures arise in realistic settings. Because practical applications prioritize a model’s input-output behaviour over its specific parameterization8,10, we further introduce functional analogues of the uncertainty exponent, based on standard measures of functional similarity24, and demonstrate that scale-insensitive irreproducibility extends to function space, as signified by near-zero functional exponents. These findings are robust across tested configurations, including different architectures, optimizers, regularization methods and activation functions. Finally, we show that the riddling framework rationalizes disparate training phenomena, including irreducible model variability6,8,9,11,12 and performance-reproducibility trade-offs17,25. Together, our results establish a robust scale-insensitive limit to reproducibility in deep learning and support riddled basin geometry as a candidate organizing principle underlying it.Neural network trainingA neural network, fθ: X → Y, is parameterized by \({\boldsymbol{\theta }}\in {{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{d}\) representing its vectorized state in parameter space. where l is the single-sample loss function. Standard training algorithms minimize the loss by iteratively updating θ. For example, the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm can be expressed as the discrete-time dynamical system, Φ, given by$$\Phi ({{\boldsymbol{\theta }}}_{t})={{\boldsymbol{\theta }}}_{t+1}={{\boldsymbol{\theta }}}_{t}-\frac{\eta }{b}\sum _{i\in {B}_{t}}{\nabla }_{{\boldsymbol{\theta }}}l({f}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta }}}({{\bf{x}}}_{i}),{{\bf{y}}}_{i}),$$

The learning rate η and mini-batch size b are hyperparameters that govern the training dynamics.Recent studies have shown that training dynamics are constrained by symmetries20,21,26,27—parameter transformations that preserve the network function. These symmetries induce invariant subspaces: trajectories starting within them remain there indefinitely. Randomly initialized networks have been observed to converge to these subspaces21, implying the presence of attractors embedded within them. Because symmetries are abundant in deep networks20, many such attractors can coexist, and numerical evidence indicates that they are chaotic16,18. Analytic results show that their stability can be weakened by large learning rates (for example, the edge of stability phenomenon25) or by negative curvatures in the loss landscape17. These three elements—symmetry-induced invariant subspaces, chaotic attractors and weakened stability—are not isolated features but interlinked. Together, these ingredients define a theoretically established route to riddling14, and given their ubiquity in deep learning, one may expect riddling could be common.Riddled basins in neural network trainingHere, we establish that neural network training can satisfy the theoretical conditions sufficient for riddling14: a chaotic attractor exists within an invariant subspace, which contains a zero-measure set of transversely unstable periodic points, together with at least one competing attractor elsewhere (see Methods for a dynamical systems primer). Because direct stability analysis of high-dimensional attractors in deep network training is analytically and computationally intractable, we adopt a minimal modelling approach. This approach, widely used in theoretical studies of deep learning18,21,28,29, provides tractability while yielding key conceptual insights.We choose our minimal model to be a two-layer network since it is the smallest architecture that admits a non-trivial symmetry: Specifically, it is an instance of the two-layer networks studied in a classic theoretical work30; we write the network function in a form that parallels their formulation$${f}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta }}}(x)={\alpha }^{(2)}{{\bf{w}}}^{(2)}\sigma ({\alpha }^{(1)}{{\bf{w}}}^{(1)}x)=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i=1}^{2}{\alpha }^{(2)}{w}_{i}^{(2)}\sigma ({\alpha }^{(1)}{w}_{i}^{(1)}x),$$
(3)
where \({\boldsymbol{\theta }}={({{\bf{w}}}^{(1)\top },{{\bf{w}}}^{(2)})}^{\top }=({w}_{1}^{(1)},{w}_{2}^{(1)},{w}_{1}^{(2)},{w}_{2}^{(2)})\in {{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{4}\) is the vector of network weights with the subscript and superscript indexing the neurons and layers, respectively. Each neuron’s weights are denoted as \({{\bf{w}}}_{i}=({w}_{i}^{(1)},{w}_{i}^{(2)})\). We use the hyperbolic tangent activation, \(\sigma =\tanh\), which under the mean field parameterization yields scaling factors30: \({\alpha }^{(1)}=\sqrt{2}\) and α(2) = 1/2. We train the network to perform regression on \(S={\{({x}_{i},{y}_{i})\}}_{i = 1}^{8}\), where \({x}_{i},{y}_{i}\sim {\mathcal N }(0,1)\). Specifically, we apply deterministic gradient descent to minimize the mean squared error, \(L({\boldsymbol{\theta }})=\)\(\frac{1}{8}{\sum }_{i=1}^{8}{({f}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta }}}({x}_{i})-{y}_{i})}^{2}\).Symmetry-induced invariant subspacesWe begin by analytically identifying invariant subspaces and training destinations in our minimal model. In total, the dynamical system governing training contains four symmetry-induced invariant subspaces (Methods). First, permutation symmetry generates a two-dimensional invariant plane, \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}}_{+}:=\{{\boldsymbol{\theta }}\in {{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{4}| {{\bf{w}}}_{1}={{\bf{w}}}_{2}\}\), where the two hidden neurons are identical. Second, the odd symmetry of the activation function (that is, \(\tanh (-x)=-\tanh (x)\)) yields an additional permutation-invariant plane, \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}}_{-}:=\{{\boldsymbol{\theta }}\in {{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{4}| {{\bf{w}}}_{1}=-{{\bf{w}}}_{2}\}\), representing a sign difference. Finally, the origin-passing activation (that is, \(\tanh (0)=0\)) induces two parity-invariant planes21, \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}}_{0}^{i}:=\{{\boldsymbol{\theta }}\in {{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{4}|\)\({{\bf{w}}}_{i}=0\}\) for i = 1, 2, corresponding to vanishing neurons. We find that the predominant competing destinations among random initializations are the permutation-invariant planes, \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}}_{\pm }\) (Extended Data Fig. 1). We assess the stability of A in terms of the longitudinal and transverse Lyapunov exponents of equation (2) (Methods). Intuitively, these exponents quantify the exponential rates of divergence on A in directions along and away from \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}}_{+}\), respectively. The longitudinal exponents converge to λ1 = 0.1564 and λ2 = 0.0256. The positive maximal exponent confirms that A is a chaotic attractor4. Conversely, the transverse exponents converge to λ3 = −0.0645 and λ4 = −0.2047. As all transverse exponents are negative, A is a Milnor attractor in the full parameter space14,31. We measure the fraction of ε-uncertain initializations, f(ε), defined as the probability that an uncertainty ε in the initialization of two otherwise identical training runs leads to differing outcomes in parameter space22,23. Thus, arbitrarily small perturbations to training can alter the training outcome with non-vanishing probability; because this sensitivity persists at all scales, increasing initialization precision—with all other factors controlled—does not materially improve reproducibility.Although some sources of stochasticity are manageable by fixing seeds (for example, initialization, mini-batch ordering, data augmentation and so on), there is often unavoidable non-deterministic perturbations, including those introduced by the computing platform (for example, GPU). In such cases, even seemingly identical training runs can produce considerable difference between network predictions6,8,10,12,34. Our results establish riddling as a potential dynamical mechanism for explaining these reproducibility limits in deep learning.Deep neural network trainingIn this section, we examine riddling-like irreproducibility in deep networks. First, we identify signatures of riddling in parameter space, including near-zero uncertainty exponents, ϕp ≈ 0. Second, we introduce functional uncertainty exponents, ϕf, as a diagnostic of reproducibility limits in function space. Third, we establish riddling analysis as a practical diagnostic framework for irreproducibility in broader settings.Parameter-space irreproducibilityIn total, we train approximately 500,000 networks spanning a wide range of training configurations, including different architectures such as VGGNet35, ResNet36 and BERT37; datasets and modalities, such as MNIST and CIFAR-10 image classification and IMDB sentiment classification; optimization algorithms, such as SGD, gradient descent and AdamW38; regularization methods, such as L1 and L2 regularization, batch and layer normalization, and dropout; and activation functions, such as \(\tanh\), ReLU and GELU. Here, we focus on a representative example: the training of the VGG-12 network with \(\tanh\) activations on the MNIST dataset corrupted with 50% label noise39, using SGD with momentum and weight decay to minimize the cross-entropy loss (Methods). This setting is computationally efficient, allowing high-resolution sampling and robust statistics. Importantly, however, the same qualitative results are observed across all configurations, including those without label noise (Supplementary Information, section 8).In this representative example, training trajectories converge to parity-invariant subspaces wherein multiple neurons in the last hidden layer vanish (Fig. 4a); see Methods for proof of invariance. To visualize the competition between different outcomes, we train a grid of networks. Beneath the heterogeneity is a diffuse structure representing the basin of attraction to the invariant subspace at θ ⋅ e⊥ = 0 (Fig. 4c). Qualitatively, this basin appears riddled; it is perforated with initializations leading elsewhere. However, parameter-space irreproducibility does not imply function-space irreproducibility due to the presence of symmetries that enable different parameter configurations to represent the same function21,41 and, for specific networks (for example, linear), imply convergence to initialization-independent solutions26. This raises the question: does functional reproducibility exhibit analogous limits?To address this question, we introduce the functional uncertainty exponent, ϕf, based on the power-law scaling of a functional similarity measure: \({m}_{\varepsilon }\propto {\varepsilon }^{{\phi }_{f}}\), where mε is the average similarity of two networks trained from ε-close initializations. Unlike the uncertainty exponent ϕp, the functional analogue ϕf does not quantify basin geometry. It diagnoses whether predictive differences diminish as initialization precision increases. Here we use churn, defined as the fraction of inputs from dataset X on which two trained networks make different predictions$${m}_{\varepsilon }({O},{{O}}^{{\prime} })={{\mathbb{E}}}_{X}\left[{{{\arg }}\max }_{j}{O}_{i,j}\ne {{{\arg }}\max }_{j}{O}_{i,j}^{{\prime} }\right],$$
(6)
where \({O},{{O}}^{{\prime} }\in {{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{N\times C}\) are output matrices of two networks, with entries Oi,j and \({O}_{i,j}^{{\prime} }\) denoting the jth class logit for the ith data input. Strikingly, increasing initialization precision does not improve functional reproducibility: the churn plateaus at approximately 2.9% and the functional exponent is indistinguishable from zero, ϕf = 0.00 ± 0.01 (Fig. 5e,f). We find consistent results across 32 functional measures from the literature24, including Cohen’s kappa42, centred kernel alignment43 and representational similarity analysis44 (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Information, section 5). Thus, scale-insensitive irreproducibility is not confined to parameter-space outcomes; functional outcomes exhibit an analogous reproducibility limit.With sufficient computational resources, our riddling analysis can be generalized to state-of-the-art networks. If network symmetries and their corresponding invariant subspaces are known, then it is possible to compute the uncertainty exponent in parameter space to ascertain evidence of riddling. In practice, this can be challenging for two reasons: First, identifying the complete set of symmetry-induced invariant subspaces is an open problem for many architectures45. Second, evaluating the training destination can be computationally intensive. For example, one must compare every possible intra-layer pair of neurons to identify the permutation-invariant subspace to which a network converges.We thus propose functional analysis as a practical and architecture-agnostic diagnostic of riddling-like behaviour. A training configuration is considered to be in a riddling-like regime when two conditions are satisfied. First, the functional uncertainty exponent is near zero. Second, nearby initializations yield substantial functional differences. Specifically, within the regime exhibiting parameter-space irreproducibility (that is, ϕp ≈ 0), we find that the magnitude of functional difference correlates strongly with generalization, irrespective of configuration details; outside it, functional differences are negligible and carry no meaningful correlation with generalization (Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Information, section 6). Applying this diagnostic systematically, we find that the signatures of riddling-like behaviour are robust to design choices spanning architecture, dataset, training algorithm, regularization and activation function (Extended Data Figs. 5 and 6 and Supplementary Information, sections 7 and 8), as well as methodological variables, including specific parameter-space slices, reference points, training horizons, thresholds and fitting ranges (Supplementary Information, section 9).Practical implications of the riddling frameworkWe next elucidate the practical implications of the riddling framework. In particular, it predicts a form of unpredictability stronger than chaos and provides a unified dynamical systems framework for understanding seemingly disparate phenomena in deep learning.Unpredictability beyond chaosThe riddling framework predicts a form of unpredictability that is radically stronger than chaos. Chaotic systems are quantitatively unpredictable: small errors grow exponentially, limiting the ability to forecast detailed trajectories. Yet they often remain qualitatively predictable since the long-term evolution stays near a single attractor. Qualitative predictability breaks down when multiple attractors compete and the boundary between their basins is fractal. In typical systems with fractal boundaries23, almost every initialization has a neighbourhood entirely contained in its basin. In such cases, the eventual destination can, in principle, be determined exactly given perfect knowledge of its initial state; that is, \({\mathrm{lim}}_{\varepsilon \to {0}^{+}}f(\varepsilon )=0\), where f(ε) denotes the probability of misclassification due to uncertainty ε in the initial state. Riddling represents a drastic departure from this. In a riddled basin, every initialization has a neighbourhood containing a positive-measure intersection of its complement14. This geometry obstructs the prediction of long-term behaviour from finite-precision information. Thus, it undermines practical applications, including safety-critical ones such as medical diagnostics8,10, which require that small changes to training do not drastically change the learned model.Irreducible model variabilityThe riddling framework also predicts that outcome variability is insensitive to the scale of differences between training runs. In practice, this is true only up to machine precision, since network parameterizations separated by less than that are represented identically. We confirm this prediction by analysing the ensemble of possible least-significant-bit flips to the reference network in Fig. 5, representing perturbations by the smallest possible amounts within machine precision. Indeed, the fraction of ε-uncertain pairs, where ε represents the least-significant bit, agrees with the near-constant value in Fig. 5: f(ε) = 0.477. Simultaneously, we observe that extrinsic perturbations, ranging from as large as seed changes to as small as floating-point errors, result in similar levels of variability in generalization (Extended Data Fig. 7), consistent with previous characterizations6,8,9,12. These results support riddling as a candidate organizing principle for irreducible model variability in deep learning.Critical learning periodsRiddling offers a geometric interpretation of the critical learning period46,47, during which sensitivity of the training outcome to perturbations is initially high and then diminishes but never vanishes12. Geometrically, sensitivity is greater when competing basins occupy a larger fraction of the neighbourhood around the network state. In Supplementary Information, section 10, we introduce a sensitivity metric \(\overline{s}\) based on this idea and conduct a control study comparing riddled and non-riddled basins. To summarize, a non-riddled basin occupies the entire space near its attractor implying vanishing sensitivity (that is, \(\bar{s}=0\)), contrary to empirical observations12. Persistent late-training sensitivity (that is, \(\bar{s}\ne 0\)) can be explained through riddling, since holes of competing basins exist arbitrarily close to the attractor.Performance-reproducibility trade-offsRiddling-like irreproducibility often coincides with the learning rate that yields peak training performance, suggesting a performance-reproducibility trade-off. At smaller learning rates, both parameter- and function-space outcomes become reproducible, but training performance deteriorates. We identify such trade-offs in the majority of tested configurations (Extended Data Figs. 6 and 8 and Supplementary Information, section 8). Similar trade-offs exist in the edge of stability (EoS)25 and chaotic training17 literature, where suppressing local instability impairs training performance. The riddling framework extends these perspectives by showing that the relevant instability is not limited to local, trajectory-level sensitivity but can also occur at the level of global functional outcomes.DiscussionIn this work, we have investigated the reproducibility of deep learning and proposed riddled basin geometry as a unifying dynamical systems mechanism underlying its limits. In a minimal model, we have shown that riddling emerges from widespread features of deep learning—symmetry20, attraction to invariant subspaces21, chaos and instability16,17,18—and produce outcome-level unpredictability, quantified by a near-zero uncertainty exponent, ϕp. With ϕp ≈ 0, increasing initialization precision does not meaningfully improve reproducibility. The same signatures arise in the parameter space of deep networks, and an analogous functional exponent, ϕf, diagnoses reproducibility limits in function space, extending the framework to settings where training destinations cannot be explicitly identified. The riddling framework thus rationalizes long-standing observations of irreproducibility5,6,7,8,9,10,11,12,48 and elevates unpredictability to be central for understanding deep learning, in parallel with other physical and computational systems4,49,50,51.Riddled basin geometry arises in a wide range of dynamical systems4,13, and local riddling, a weaker property, was previously reported in simple networks trained on chaotic time series52. We expect riddling could be widespread because its ingredients are prevalent in deep learning. Even when the conditions for riddling are only partially met, riddled-like behaviours can persist53,54,55,56,57. Indeed, in the minimal model, we have observed a sequence of phase transitions as the learning rate increases, from no riddling to pseudo-riddling (a mixture of riddled and non-riddled components), true riddling and transient riddling (Extended Data Fig. 9 and Supplementary Information, section 1). Empirically, we have found riddling-like reproducibility limits across a range of test configurations, including VGGNet, ResNet and BERT trained with different optimizers, regularizers and activation functions (Supplementary Information, section 8). Together with related observations of training instability in diverse settings, including large language models and recurrent neural networks9,11,12, these findings support riddling as a potential unifying mechanism for irreproducibility in deep learning.The riddling framework complements EoS viewpoints18,25,48 by addressing the global organization of training outcomes rather than only local trajectory-level instability. EoS involves instability along high-curvature directions and provides a route to weakened transverse stability or chaotic dynamics (Supplementary Information, section 11). However, riddling additionally requires competing attractors in symmetry-induced invariant subspaces. These additional ingredients produce qualitative unpredictability4, which is stronger than what can be understood through EoS phenomena alone. The riddling perspective thus yields a distinct prediction: systems exhibiting similar EoS behaviour may nevertheless differ in reproducibility due to differences in their invariant subspace or attractor structure. This prediction motivates interventions beyond simply reducing the learning rate, including symmetry-breaking strategies. Consistent with this prediction, symmetry removal can mitigate the initialization-dependence of training outcomes58, although the resulting basin geometry remains to be characterized, as destinations are no longer identifiable through matched or vanishing neurons.Our results further suggest a trade-off between training performance and reproducibility: near-zero parameter- and function-space uncertainty exponents often coincide with the optimal learning rate (Supplementary Information, section 8). What factors determine whether performance and irreproducibility coincide? Can riddling be analytically connected to generalization bounds, for example, through algorithmic stability59? In Supplementary Information, section 6, we identify trends in this direction: in the riddling-like regime, the generalization error is strongly correlated with the functional difference between networks trained from ε-close initializations, independent of training details. Outside this regime, by contrast, functional differences are near zero and uncorrelated with generalization error. Given the conventional view that generalization is related to the flatness of a solution60, the relationship between irreproducibility and the structure of the loss landscape warrants further investigation.As deep learning advances into domains where reproducibility is vital, substantial effort has been dedicated to managing the variability caused by non-deterministic software and hardware5,6,7,8,10,11,12,34,61,62,63. Yet, the mechanism by which small perturbations yield large network differences remained unexplored. Early work showed that back-propagation is sensitive to initial conditions64, with convergence-rate maps exhibiting fractal structures, as also found recently in hyperparameter space15 (see Supplementary Information, section 3 for connections between parameter-space riddling and hyperparameter-space fractality resembling lakes of Wada65). Those studies, however, concerned ordinary ‘skinny’ fractals with zero Lebesgue measure. By contrast, our analysis of destination maps uncovers ‘fat’ fractals, in the form of riddled basins, with positive Lebesgue measure66: the basin of attraction for one destination is densely intertwined with points belonging to others. Unlike skinny fractality, which degrades reproducibility only near basin boundaries and can be overcome by increasing precision, fat fractality sets a scale-insensitive limit: an arbitrarily small perturbation to any initialization can change the basin in which it resides, and no increase in precision offers recourse. Our findings are thus consistent with the interpretation that irreproducibility in deep learning arises not from perturbations per se but from their coupling with riddled basin geometry.More broadly, riddling entails a form of unpredictable dynamics that is qualitatively new to neural network training, and in complexity, exceeds the chaotic behaviours studied previously16,17,18. In idealized dynamical systems with riddled or intermingled basins, related undecidability phenomena can arise, and similar behaviour was recently demonstrated in quantum many-body systems with phase diagrams exhibiting fractal structure51,67,68. Our results show a practical obstruction to robust prediction under finite perturbations, consistent with this dynamical systems picture. Deep learning thus joins this broader context, with riddled basin geometry emerging as a candidate organizing principle for irreproducibility in modern AI.MethodsA dynamical systems primerHere, we define concepts from dynamical systems theory that are relevant for riddled basins. Riddling requires a measure-theoretical definition of an attractor31. Consider a dynamical system whose time dependence is generated by the iteration of a map \(\varPhi :{{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{d}\to {{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{d}\). Suppose there exists an invariant set \(A\subset {{\mathbb{R}}}^{d}\), such that Φt(A) ⊂ A for all t. The basin of attraction of A is \(\beta (A):=\{{\boldsymbol{\theta }}\in {{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{d}| \omega ({\boldsymbol{\theta }})\subset A\}\), where the ω-limit set \(\omega ({\boldsymbol{\theta }}):={\cap }_{t > 0}\overline{\{{\varPhi }^{s}({{\boldsymbol{\theta }}}_{0})| s > t\}}\) is the set of accumulation points of the trajectory Φt(θ0) as t → ∞. That is, β(A) contains all points that accumulate in A. The invariant set A is a Milnor attractor if l(β(A)) > 0 and \(l(\beta (A){\setminus}\beta ({A}^{{\prime} })) > 0\) for any proper compact subset \({A}^{{\prime} }\subset A\), where l is the d-dimensional Lebesgue measure. In contrast to other definitions of an attractor, the basin of a Milnor attractor need not contain an open neighbourhood of the attractor itself. Milnor attractors are essential for the formulation of riddled basins, as riddling can occur even arbitrarily close to the attractor, violating classical notions of Lyapunov stability. A basin of attraction β(A) is riddled if for all θ ∈ β(A) and δ > 0 we have \(l({B}_{\delta }({\boldsymbol{\theta }})\cap \beta {(A)}^{c}) > 0\), where Bδ(θ) denotes the δ-neighbourhood of θ (ref. 14). Thus any initialization attracted to A is arbitrarily close to another initialization leading to a different attractor.As established in the dynamical systems theory, the theoretical conditions sufficient for riddling are: the existence of a chaotic attractor within an invariant subspace, containing a zero measure set of transversely unstable periodic points and at least one competing attractor elsewhere. We now clarify these conditions: a subspace \({\mathcal{P}}\) is invariant if trajectories originating within the subspace remain in it indefinitely (that is, \(\varPhi ({\mathscr{ \mathcal P }})\subset {\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}\)). Within the invariant subspace is a chaotic attractor A, meaning that there exists a basin β(A) of initializations off the subspace that are drawn towards A. Under the classical definition of chaos, a chaotic attractor contains periodic points; a point is periodic if by taking a finite number of steps from it, the system would return to the point (that is, Φm(θ) = θ). We regard periodic points in the chaotic attractor as atypical as they constitute a set of measure zero. These periodic points are transversely unstable if small transverse perturbations from them grow over time. Through local stability analysis17, the transverse instability of a point can occur if in its vicinity the curvature of the loss function in the transverse direction is either negative or large relative to the learning rate; the latter is related to the edge of stability phenomenon25 (see Supplementary Information, section 11 for experimental evidence).We now illustrate how these conditions constitute the standard dynamical mechanism for riddling (see ref. 32 for a classical example). The chaotic attractor within the invariant subspace, \(A\subset {\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}\), has a basin of attraction β(A), so a positive volume of initial conditions off the subspace converges towards A. However, the transverse instability of a periodic point P embedded in A implies that, simultaneously, there are initializations arbitrarily close to the invariant subspace that are repelled away from it. The presence of competing attractors then converts these ejected trajectories into different long-term outcomes. In other words, such ejected trajectories may follow heteroclinic connections towards a competing attractor, for example one located in another invariant subspace, such as \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}}_{-}\) in the minimal model, or at infinity. If P also has stable directions, this trajectory aligns with a stable manifold funneling nearby points towards the same destination. The set of initial conditions that converge to the competing attractor can thus be visualized as a ‘hyperwedge’ anchored at the periodic point (see the schematic in Extended Data Fig. 2). Because pre-images of these points also evolve towards the same competing attractor, the hyperwedge structure is reproduced at the pre-iterates of P. Owing to the chaotic dynamics on A, these pre-iterates are dense in the attractor. Consequently, a dense collection of hyperwedges is generated throughout the basin. These hyperwedges perforate β(A), producing the characteristic fat-fractal geometry of a basin that is densely riddled with initial conditions leading elsewhere.Chaotic attractor visualizationTo visualize the chaotic attractor in the permutation-invariant subspace \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}}_{+}\), we train the network for 105 epochs from a random initialization inside \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}}_{+}\). Accordingly, we design a training configuration that is realistic in the sense that we maximize the complexity of the architecture and learning task under constrained compute (for example, experiments are replicable within one week on a high performance computing cluster). We use a VGG-12 network, which is a 12-layer implementation of the VGG architecture that is widely used for image classification35. The VGG-12 comprises nine convolutional layers and three fully connected layers. To facilitate faster training, we taper the network to 12,036 parameters by reducing the number of channels per layer and removing biases. Bias removal also induces a symmetry that we exploit to render higher resolution visualizations (see the following sections). Networks are trained to perform image classification on the MNIST dataset corrupted with 50% label noise (that is, half of the training data is intentionally mislabeled). We note that there is a vast literature devoted to label noise as it is a ubiquitous issue in practical machine learning39. The following section explains the symmetries that enable this shortcut.Symmetry-induced invariant subspacesAn affine subspace is invariant when the neural network is reflection-symmetric around it21. Although this symmetry need only be approximate (that is, in a neighbourhood of the subspace), it is exact for the permutation- and parity-invariant subspaces considered in this work. Here, we establish three results.First, a neural network with an odd activation function σ is reflection-symmetric across an affine subspace \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}}_{0}^{J}\) with set J indexing multiple neurons in the same hidden layer l. This generalizes the single-neuron case (that is, ∣J∣ = 1)21. A reflection across \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}}_{0}^{J}\) flips the sign of parameters of neurons in J, including the incoming weights w(l), outgoing weights w(l+1) and biases b(l) of each neuron. The input to the hidden layer x(l−1) is unchanged. As a result, their activations σ(w(l) ⋅ x(l−1) + b(l)) flip sign (because σ is odd). This is cancelled by the sign flip of the outgoing weights, leaving the neural network output invariant. Although there exists other parity-invariant subspaces (for example, sets J indexing neurons of different layers that do not share weights), the result here encompasses the vast majority (≈99.2%) of the destinations observed in VGG-12 network training.Second, if in addition the neural network has an even number of hidden layers and no bias parameters, then it is reflection-symmetric across the affine subspace \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal N }}}_{0}^{J}\) that is transverse to \({{\mathcal{P}}}_{0}^{J}\). This subspace corresponds to all parameters not belonging to neurons in set J vanishing. A reflection across \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal N }}}_{0}^{J}\) reverses the sign of these parameters. As a result, a (−1) factor is accrued at each hidden layer before and after the lth hidden layer, as well as the output layer. Note that the lth hidden layer does not contribute a factor. To see this, note that the input to the lth hidden layer changes as x(l−1) ↦ (−1)l−1x(l−1). For neurons in J, their activations become (−1)(l−1)σ(w(l) ⋅ x(l−1)). For neurons not in J, their activations become (−1)(l)σ(w(l) ⋅ x(l−1)) because w(l) ↦ − w(l). Another sign flip at the outgoing weights of neurons not in J cancels this additional factor. The total factor accrued at the neural network output is \({(-1)}^{{l}_{{\rm{total}}}}\), where ltotal is the total number of hidden layers. Thus, a neural network is reflection-symmetric across \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal N }}}_{0}^{J}\) if it has an even number of hidden layers and no bias parameters. Under these conditions, \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal N }}}_{0}^{J}\) is an invariant subspace21. Since the VGG-12 network satisfies these conditions, the result implies the left–right symmetry of Fig. 4b,c.Third, a neural network with an odd activation is reflection-symmetric across additional subspaces \({{\mathscr{ \mathcal P }}}_{-}^{i,j}:=\{{\boldsymbol{\theta }}\in {{{{\mathbb{R}}}}}^{d}| {{\bf{w}}}_{i}=-{{\bf{w}}}_{j}\}\), where wi and wj are the vectorized parameters of the i and j neurons in the same hidden layer. Reflection across this subspace corresponds to the composition of a permutation of parameters and a sign flip.
